newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Delays seen in Brazil's telecom sell-offs in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Delays seen in Brazil's telecom sell-offs in 1997.

text.p: Brazil hopes to make substantial headway this year in the privatization of its large, promising telecom sector, but progress is likely to be slower than expected, analysts said.
"The government is being optimistic with its timetable," said Jacopo Valentino of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Brazil.
Government officials plan to take bids March 31 on concessions to operate on the B Band cellular frequency and expect to begin the sale of federally owned Telebras before year's end.

However, analysts said the planned schedule may be wishful thinking, and delays can be expected given the government's track record on privatizations and the vast amounts of money involved in the sell-offs.
After China, Brazil is seen as the world's most promising untapped telecommunications markets and its planned privatization has drawn the interest of virtually every global telecom player.
The auction process is slated to begin this year with the granting of cellular concessions and the break-up of the federal Telebras system into four regional units and long-distance unit Embratel.

Although no formal timetable is set, Communications Minister Sergio Motta said the government plans to auction off Embratel and the largest Telebras unit, Telesp, this year and the rest of the federal giant by the end of 1998.
Analysts, however, said the first sales of Telebras' regional units are not likely to occur before 1998's second quarter.
"It's possible, but not probable. It seems a little bit optimistic," said Maxim Medvedovsky of Banco Icatu.
The likely snag? Approval of Brazil's new General Telecommunications Law, which the government hopes to push through Congress by April.

The law would create a regulatory watchdog, set rules for the sector and outline Telebras' sale. But it is likely to fall victim to Brazil's slow-moving political process, now hampered by uncertainty on the fate of the government's re-election drive, and approval may not come before the second half of 1997, analysts said.

Meanwhile, investors eyeing the 10 B Band cellular concessions up for grabs are likely to request extensions beyond March 31 to allow them more time to study and prepare bids, something common in Brazil's privatization program.
"These are going to be complex proposals and we're talking about a lot of money," Valentino said.
The government Monday released bid specifications setting some 3.7 billion reais in base prices, as well as payment terms, minimum numbers of lines to be installed and other bidding details.

Valentino said plans to start awarding 15-year concession contracts in May or June also may be pushed back as the dates coincide with the time courts will be ruling on legal challenges to the telecom sale by leftist political parties.
"It is a delicate time," he added.
